source_text: Principalis itaque et exinde tota congressio de numero, an duos deos liceat induci, si forte, poetica et pictoria licentia, et tertia iam, haeretica. sed ueritas Christiana destricte pronuntiauit: deus si non unus est, non est, quia dignius credimus non esse quodcumque non ita fuerit, ut esse debebit. deum autem ut scias unum esse debere, quaere quid sit deus, et non aliter inuenies. quantum humana condicio de deo definire potest, id definio, quod et omnium conscientia agnoscet: deum summum esse magnum in aeternitate constitutum, [innatum, infectum, sine initio, sine-fine] — hunc enim statum aeternitati t censendum, quae summum magnum deum efficiat, dum hoc est in deo ipsa — atque ita et cetera, ut sit deus summum magnum et forma et ratione et ui et potestate. cum de isto conuenit apud omnes, — nemo enim negabit deum summum magnum quid esse, nisi qui potuerit deum imum modicum quid e contrario pronuntiare, ut deum neget auferendo quod dei est - quae erit iam condicio ipsius summi magni? nempe, ut nihil illi adaequetur, id est, ut non sit aliud summum magnum, quia, si fuerit, adaequabitur, et si adaequabitur, non erit iam summum magnum, euersa condicione et, ut ita dixerim, lege, quae summo magno nihil sinit adaequari. ergo unicum sit necesse est summum magnum, — quod fuerit par non habendo — ne non sit summum magnum. ergo non aliter erit quam per quod habet esse, id est unicum omnino. proinde deus cum summum magnum sit, recte ueritas nostra pronuntiauit: deus, si non. unus est, non est, non quasi dubitemus esse deum dicendo: si non unus, non est, sed quia quem confidimus esse, id eum definiamus esse, quod si non est, deus non est. [et summum scilicet magnum] porro (si) summum magnum unicum sit necesse est, ergo et deus unicus erit, non aliter deus, nisi summum magnum, nec aliter summum magnum, nisi parem non habens, nec aliter parem non habens, nisi unicus fuerit. certe quemcumque alium deum induxeris, non alia poteris eum forma tueri deum quam ut et illi proprium diuinitatis adscripseris, sicut aeternum ita et summum magnum. duo ergo summa magna quomodo consistent, cum hoc sit summum magnum, par non habere, par autem non habere uni competat, in duobus esse nullo modo possit?
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, the main and subsequent entire discussion is about the number, whether it is permissible to introduce two gods, if perhaps by poetic and pictorial license, and now also heretical. But Christian truth has pronounced distinctly: if God is not one, He is not, because we believe it is more worthy not to be whatever is not as it ought to be. But so that you may know God ought to be one, seek what God is, and you will not find otherwise. As much as human condition can define God, I define this, which also everyone's conscience will acknowledge: God is the highest, great, established in eternity, without beginning, without end — for this state is to be reckoned to eternity, which makes God the highest great God, while this is in God Himself — and thus also the rest, so that God is the highest great one in form and reason and power. Since everyone agrees about this, no one will deny that God is the highest great one, unless someone can pronounce the contrary, that God is the lowest minor thing, so that he denies God by taking away what is of God. What will be the condition of this highest great one? Namely, that nothing equals it, that is, that there is no other highest great one, because if there is, it will equal, and if it equals, it will not be the highest great one, with the condition overturned and, so to speak, the law which allows nothing to equal the highest great one. Therefore, it is necessary that the highest great one is unique, which has no equal — lest it not be the highest great one. Therefore, it will not be otherwise than through what it has to be, that is, unique altogether. Accordingly, since God is the highest great one, our truth has pronounced rightly: if God is not one, He is not, not as if we doubt whether God exists, saying 'if not one, He is not,' but because we define what we confess God to be, what if it is not, God is not. Furthermore, if the highest great one must be unique, therefore God will also be unique, not otherwise God, unless the highest great one, not otherwise the highest great one, unless having no equal, not otherwise having no equal, unless it is unique. Certainly, whichever other god you introduce, you will not be able to preserve him as God in any other form than by ascribing to him also the property of divinity, just as eternal, so also the highest great one. Therefore, how can two highest great ones coexist, since this is the highest great one, to have no equal, and to have no equal belongs to one, and cannot be in two?
pass_b_english: So the whole debate comes down to numbers: whether we're allowed to posit two gods — maybe by poetic license, maybe by artistic license, and now, heretical license too. But Christian truth calls it straight: if God isn't one, God isn't. Period. Because we hold it more fitting that nothing exists at all than that something exists in a way it shouldn't.

Want to know why God has to be one? Ask what God is. You won't find any other answer. As far as human language can stretch, here's the definition — and every conscience will back me up: God is the supreme greatness, fixed in eternity, unborn, unending. That's what eternity means: the very condition that makes God supremely great, because that condition *is* God. And from that flows everything else — God is supreme in form, in reason, in power.

Everyone agrees on this — no one denies God is the supreme greatness, unless they're ready to call God the lowest trifle instead, which is just denying God by stripping away what makes God God. So what defines the supreme greatness? Simple: nothing equals it. Which means there *can't* be another supreme greatness. Because if there were, they'd be equals. And if they're equals, neither is supreme. The whole definition collapses — the law, if you will, that lets nothing stand alongside the supreme.

So the supreme greatness *must* be unique — no equal, or it stops being supreme. It exists *as* unique; that's the only way it exists at all. And since God *is* the supreme greatness, our truth got it right: if God isn't one, God isn't. Not that we're hedging — 'maybe God doesn't exist if not one.' No. We're defining the God we trust: this is what God *is*. If that's not true, God isn't.

So if the supreme greatness has to be unique, God has to be unique. God isn't God unless supreme; supreme isn't supreme unless peerless; peerless isn't peerless unless unique. Try smuggling in another god — you'll have to give him every divine attribute: eternal, supreme, the works. Then you've got two supreme greatnesses. How does that work? The definition of supreme is *having no peer*. That's a singular property. Two things can't both have no peer. They'd be each other's peer. Contradiction. Game over.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex logical structure of the Latin text, particularly the conditional arguments regarding the definition of 'summum magnum' (supreme greatness) and the necessity of uniqueness. Pass A preserves all clauses and nuances, including the bracketed text. Pass B provides a fluent rendering that maintains the theological and logical integrity of the source without adding external meaning or omitting the author's distinctions.
